description:
Corrections applied to EF 3.1 flows as they are extracted from the ILCD archive, and again as the transform reads them back, before anything downstream sees them. Same shape as every other *-manual-fixes.json and applied by the same code.

Most of the entries below are a code table for #19: EF 3.1 names 55 refrigerants, blowing agents and heat-transfer fluids by ASHRAE or industry designation and gives them no identifier of any kind, so no resolver can place them -- OPSIN parses IUPAC names and a designation is not one, and the PubChem and ChEBI enrichment is keyed on a CAS these flows do not have. A designation is a complete specification, so the identity is recoverable, but only from a table someone can audit.

Each entry states its evidence. The designation was accepted for a PubChem record only when that record lists the designation among its own synonyms, so the code-to-compound link is PubChem's assertion and not arithmetic done here.

Twenty of the entries are a second code table for the same issue, and they exist because that acceptance rule ran out. For twenty-one designations PubChem holds no record carrying the code at all, so there was nothing to cite and the first pass stopped. What answers for them is the characterisation factor. EF 3.1's `Climate change` category is a transcription of IPCC AR6 WGI Table 7.SM.7, and that table prints, on one line, the industry designation, the chemical structure and the GWP100. So a flow EF names only by a code still carries a number that names a row of a published table, and the row states the structure the code stands for. `HFE-143a` is the worked example: EF characterises it at 616 kg CO2-eq per kilogram, AR6's `HFE-143a` row is CH3OCF3 at 616, and PubChem's record for CH3OCF3 is CAS 421-14-7. Nothing in that chain decodes the digits. Every GWP100 quoted below was read from the published Chapter 7 Supplementary Material at https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_Chapter07_SM.pdf, not from the government-distribution draft that circulates as a standalone extract of the same table; the two agree on every GWP column and differ only in the two absolute-GTP columns, which nothing here reads.

The factor is evidence rather than decoration, and it is what makes this table safer than a name search rather than more speculative. `HFE-143a` and `HFC-143a` are different substances that a search engine will happily confuse -- the second is 1,1,1-trifluoroethane, CH3CF3, 420-46-2, and AR6 gives it 5810 against the first's 616 -- and it is the factor, not the name, that tells them apart. The same check separates the two 1234ze isomers, whose stereo-unspecified parent record carries both isomers' designations in one synonym list, and it is what says EF's two perfluorodecalin rows are two substances (AR6's 7800 and 7120) rather than one entered twice.

Where the factor identifies a substance EF 3.1 already publishes under its chemical name, the two sets of flows share a flow object, which is the same duplicate-entry outcome `PFC-1114` and `PFC-51-14` already have. Six of the twenty do that: `HFE-143a`, `HFE-216`, `Halon-2301`, `(Z)-HFC-1336`, `n-HFE-7200`, and the damaged label that turns out to be `HG-02`.

One of the twenty-one is deliberately not here. `i-HFE-7200` is CAS 163702-06-5, and EF 3.1 already carries that number on its `HFE-7200` flow, which is the commercial product -- a mixture of the n- and i- ethers. Asserting it would merge a mixture with one of its components, which is worse than leaving the designation unidentified, and the underlying defect is EF's number on the mixture rather than anything this table can fix. Where the digits do decode -- the halocarbon series encode carbon, hydrogen and fluorine counts -- the predicted formula was compared with the one PubChem reports, and a disagreement was treated as blocking rather than resolved in either direction. Series are not mixed: `HFE-143a` and `HFC-143a` share a number and are different substances, and `(E)-` and `(Z)-` isomers are different substances with different CAS numbers, so neither was matched against the other or against a stereo-unspecified parent.

Seventy of the entries are a second pass over the same family, and they change a name rather than supply a number (#104). EF 3.1 publishes 118 substances under an industry part number -- `HFC-134a`, `CFC-12`, `Halon-1301`, counted on the 2026-08-17 build at commit 87a5918 -- and this project has already ruled twice that a part number is a worse published name than the chemistry. The rule that would propose the rename cannot reach any of them: it acts only where Common Chemistry and ChEBI both name the registry number, and ChEBI, a database of biologically interesting molecules, answers for six of the 118. Rather than trust one database where the other is silent, the renames a curator is confident of are written here one at a time, and the other 48 keep the part number.

A rename is written down only where all of five things hold: the substance carries exactly one registry number; Common Chemistry names it; no other designation in the list carries the same number; that name is a chemical name and not another designation or the inverted CAS index form; and the name fixes the same structure the designation does, which for a name carrying no locants means the molecule admits only one arrangement. Each entry says which of those needed saying. Every one of the seventy sets `retain_original_as_synonym`, so the part number stays searchable -- an inventory written against EF 3.1 holds no other string for the substance.

Where Common Chemistry and ChEBI both answer and differ only in style -- systematic against common, `Trifluoromethane` against `fluoroform` -- the published name is the one other contributing lists use. That is a repo rule (AGENTS.md 35) and not a pattern in code: which of two names is the common one is not a question a string can be asked. It settles three of the six disagreements in this family, and in all three ecoinvent 3.12 names the substance and agrees with itself across both other sources.

One thing to know before adding another. A name written here is the *source* name, so `normalize_name_case` sees it and title-cases every word with no capital beyond the first: `Methyl perfluoroisopropyl ether` is published as `Methyl Perfluoroisopropyl Ether`. Two of the seventy come out that way and the rest do not, because a name carrying locants or a single word is left alone. That is the list's prevailing style rather than something these entries introduce -- 1,821 of the 2,046 multi-word labels on the 2026-08-17 build are title-cased the same way, and the 225 that are not are the ones `consensus_match` renamed after the caser had run. It is recorded here because the alternative reading, that the entry got the capitalisation wrong, is the one a reader will reach for first.

fixes.comment: 232-319-8 is the EINECS number for pyrethrins, the natural insecticidal mixture extracted from chrysanthemum. Jasmolin I is one constituent of that mixture, not the mixture, and has its own CAS (4466-14-2) and formula (C21H30O3). An identifier for a mixture is not an identity claim about a constituent. Carrying it here makes the EC index assert that Jasmolin I and Jasmolin II are the same substance, so ecoinvent's `Pyrethrins` flow (CAS 8003-34-7, EC 232-319-8) resolves to two flow objects and is reported as `multiple-flow-object-candidates` in six contexts. Matched on CAS because EF 3.1 repeats the substance once per context, 13 flows in total. The CAS numbers are correct and are left alone.

The same mixture EC number on the other constituent. Jasmolin II is the methyl-ester homologue of Jasmolin I -- distinct CAS (1172-63-0), distinct formula (C22H30O5) -- and shares nothing with it but the mixture they both occur in. Removing the EC from both is what leaves the pair distinguishable. Also 13 flows, one per context.

8006-14-2 is natural gas's registry number, and this flow is not natural gas. Gas that seeps out of a coal seam while the coal is being mined comes out of a mine rather than a gas field, and EF 3.1 says as much itself, on the neighbouring `Pit Methane` flow: "Pit methane is a different substance than natural gas (impurities, heating value etc.)". EF keeps the two substances apart three ways -- by name, by category (this one is a *material* resource from ground, natural gas an *energy* resource) and by unit (m3 against MJ) -- and the registry number is the single thing they share. It is also the only one of the four that decides identity downstream, so it is the only one that does damage. The number is not EF's own: this row is a copy of the ILCD reference elementary flow, entered 2012-01-20, and carries it from there. ecoinvent, whose flow name this is, shipped the same error and has already corrected it -- 3.8 and 3.9.1 put 8006-14-2 on this substance, 3.10.1 and every version after it leave it off, under the same UUID -- and the same removal is stated in ecoinvent-3.8-manual-fixes.json and ecoinvent-3.9.1-manual-fixes.json. What the number cost was eight synonyms: enrichment looked it up and wrote natural gas's names onto coal-mine gas, so `Natural gas`, `Gas, natural` and `Sweet natural gas` named two flow objects at once and BAFU's two natural gas rows could be placed on neither. (#80)

A standard cubic metre, because that is what this gas is measured in everywhere else. EF 3.1 ships this flow with the Volume flow property and `m3`, inherited from the ILCD reference elementary flow it copies; ecoinvent, whose name this is, gives the same substance in `m3` at 3.8 and relabels it `Sm3` from 3.9 under an unchanged UUID, and BAFU reports its two rows in `m3` and `Nm3`. A cubic metre of gas is not a quantity until the temperature and pressure it was measured at are stated, which is the whole difference between the two spellings: `units.json` reads `m3` as a volume and `sm3` as an amount of substance, 42.38 mol at 15 degrees and 1 atm per ISO 91:2017. So the bare volume is the reading that cannot be right for a gas resource, and following ecoinvent's own relabelling is what puts the lists in one unit.

The factor is 1.0 and is stated rather than assumed: this is a relabelling of what EF already meant, not a rescaling of anybody's amounts, and without the number the rewrite would be a silent reinterpretation of them. `units.json` implies nothing between the two -- they are different quantity kinds -- so 1.0 is a claim it could not have made for itself. What it claims is that EF's cubic metre on this flow was always gas at the conditions ecoinvent states. (#80)

The other half of the same correction, and the half that says what the number is for. EF 3.1 gives natural gas no identifier at all -- 8006-14-2 appears exactly once in the whole of EF 3.1, on the coal-mine off-gas above. The build does not leave that gap open: `commonchem_cas_review` looks the flow's name up and fills the number in from Common Chemistry's exact-name match, which is how the object carries it today. That is the right number arrived at by the wrong route -- a live lookup against a changeable service, recorded as a fill-in rather than as something this project asserts, and invisible in the diff a reviewer reads. Stated here it is curated data with its evidence attached, and the move off coal-mine gas and onto natural gas reads as the single decision it is. The number is natural gas's wherever it is used: Common Chemistry's preferred name for 8006-14-2 is `Natural gas`, ECHA lists it as EC 232-343-9 `Natural gas`, and ecoinvent carries it on `Gas, natural` in every version from 3.9.1 through 3.12. This row has been stripped of identifying material once before -- its own comment reads "synonyms were erroneous; removed" -- and this puts back the one identifier that is not in doubt. (#80)

`HFC-1234yf` is a typo for `HFO-1234yf`. The 1234yf designation names an olefin -- 2,3,3,3-tetrafluoropropene, the leading digit of a four-digit refrigerant number being its count of double bonds -- and the HFC family is by definition saturated, so the compound cannot be an HFC. HFO is the prefix the industry uses for it and the one EF 3.1 itself uses elsewhere: the `polyhaloalkene` flow, which is this same substance, carries `hfo-1234yf` in its own synonym list. The misspelling is common enough that PubChem records `HFC 1234yf` as a synonym of CID 2776731, which is how #19 resolved the flow in the first place; that makes it findable, not correct. One of 5 flows carrying this name, 26 characterisation factors between them. (#19)

Palladium is Pd, atomic number 46, and its heaviest known isotope is around mass 128: there is no Pd-234, so there is no Pd-234m. This is protactinium-234m -- Pa-234m, the short-lived isomer in the uranium-238 decay chain, and one of the nuclides an LCA inventory is most likely to report. The symbol `Pa` was expanded to the wrong element name. Twelve flows, all kBq, all in radiological release contexts -- air at ground level, aircraft cruise height, high stack, ocean, surface water, agricultural ground -- and a palladium flow measured in becquerels across those contexts is not a palladium flow. EF 3.1 half-knows: the general comment on all twelve reads `CAS No and Synonyms removed; were erroneous. Correct CAS to be identified. Possibly has none assigned.` The identifiers were withdrawn because they did not match the name; the name that made them not match was left in place, and the flow arrives here carrying no CAS at all. With the label corrected the isotope lookup finds `234Pam` and the object types as Isotope and Radionuclide, where before it was untyped for `no_structure_and_no_registry_identifier` -- see #20. Pa-234m keeps its own flow object rather than merging with `Protactinium-234` (CAS 15100-28-4): they are different nuclides with different half-lives, and the nuclide identity is what now holds them apart.

7440-61-1 is the registry number for *uranium*, the element. U-238's own is 24678-82-8. Both EF 3.1 and ecoinvent ship the element's number on their uranium-238 rows, and nothing in this pipeline put it there. Keying a nuclide by its nuclide already stops the CAS deciding which flow object these rows land on (#17), so this changes no grouping; what it changes is what the object publishes. Left alone, an object labelled `Uranium-238` and typed `chemrof:Isotope` goes out asserting the element's registry number, and any consumer joining on CAS re-merges what the layering separated. The same is true of `thorium-232` and `Praseodym-147`, which carry 7440-29-1 and 7440-10-0; those two are left as they are because this project has no cited nuclide-specific number for them, and inventing one would be worse than publishing the vendor's.

`Praseodym` is a truncation of the element name, and truncations are corrected here rather than absorbed by the nuclide parser: a parser that accepts prefixes would accept the next wrong one too. Only one element begins `Praseodym`, so the reading is not in doubt, and the mass number is EF's own claim -- Pr-147 exists, with a half-life of 13.39 minutes and beta decay, which is consistent with a fission-product flow reported in becquerels. Left uncorrected the label matched nothing, and the fallback that searched the object's synonyms answered with `Praseodymium-141` -- the *stable* natural isotope, `IS=100%` -- so a becquerel flow was published as a nuclide that does not decay. The flow also carries CAS 7440-10-0, which is elemental praseodymium's; that is why it shared a flow object with the element's kg flows, and keying a nuclide by its nuclide is what separates them (#17).

Silver-110 is the 24.56-second ground state; the species a reactor-effluent inventory reports is the isomer, Ag-110m, at 249.863 days. Both lists write the bare name and neither carries a separate Silver-110m row, so this is a shared vendor convention rather than one list's slip and cannot be resolved by preferring the other list -- the same correction is in ecoinvent-3.12-manual-fixes.json (#24). The half-life alone cannot settle it: 49 of the 81 matched isotope objects publish a half-life under a year and most of them are legitimate, Krypton-89 at 3.15 minutes among them. What settles it is that EF states which nuclide it means a second time, in its own characterisation factor. The four water rows carry `Ionising radiation, human health` at 0.0236 kBq U235-eq per kBq. Twenty-one nuclides in this list carry a water factor under that method and not one of them is short-lived: the band runs from Iodine-129 at 4.71 down to Strontium-90 at 0.000193, and this factor sits between Antimony-124 (60.2 d) and Manganese-54 (312 d), equal to Iodine-131's. A human exposure efficiency of that size needs a nuclide that survives long enough to reach an ingestion pathway, and a 24.56-second beta emitter discharged to the ocean does not. The factor was computed for the isomer. Against that, the row's synonyms include `110Ag`, which reads as the ground state -- but they are PubChem's synonym set for the CAS, which lists `110nAg` and `Silver-110n` in the same breath, so it is not an independent claim. The CAS is deliberately left alone: 14391-76-5 is indexed as `Silver, isotope of mass 110`, which names a mass number rather than a nuclear state, so it neither corroborates nor contradicts the corrected label, and there is no cited number for the isomer to put in its place. 12 flows, all kBq, across the radiological release contexts. With the label corrected the isotope lookup resolves the bare `m` to the longest-lived excited state -- PubChem files that as `110Agn` at 249.863 days and gives `110Agm` to a 660-nanosecond state no inventory reports -- so this fix depends on `_resolve_metastable_state` in flow_layers/elements.py and would publish a worse record than it replaced without it.  `Silver-110` is retained as an alternative label: it is not a wrong name, it is the name both vendor lists ship for this substance, and correcting the preferred one to `Silver-110m` otherwise deletes the only string a consumer holding one of those inventories can search the published list for.

EF 3.1 points this flow at the wrong flow property, and the unit is derived from the one it points at. Its `flowProperty` references 93a60a56-a3c8-11da-a746-0800200c9a66, which resolves to 'Net calorific value' in units of energy -- while the `shortDescription` EF wrote beside that very reference reads 'Radioactivity', and every other EF 3.1 radionuclide (Krypton-85m, Uranium alpha) references 93a60a56-a3c8-17da-a746-0800200c9a66, the actual Radioactivity property. The two uuids differ in one hex digit. So MJ is a faithful read of a pointer EF mistyped, not a decision EF made. Actinium is a trace decay product of uranium ore, not an energy carrier, and no calorific value for it exists to be meant.

The property is dropped rather than corrected to Radioactivity because EF supplies no number to correct it with: actinium's only flowProperty carries meanValue 1.0, the degenerate self-reference every one of the 94,062 EF 3.1 flows has, so there is no calorific value and no activity on the record either. With the property gone the unit comes from the mapping instead -- ecoinvent gives `Actinium, in ground` in kg in 3.8 and `Actinium` in kg in 3.12, and EF's own classification puts the flow under 'Resources from ground'. kg is what both sides already agree the flow measures.

Safe to change: the flow uuid appears in none of the 25 EF 3.1 LCIA methods, so nothing characterises it and no score can move. Before this the pair was the one finding `merge.unit_changes` reported that was a genuine defect rather than an accepted mapping, in both ecoinvent 3.8 and 3.12; it is deliberately not in unit-change-allowlist.json, because accepting kg onto MJ would have recorded the mistyped pointer as a decision.

The classification is left alone. 'Non-renewable energy resources from ground' is wrong for actinium in the same way the unit was, but the context is what pairs this flow with ecoinvent's, and changing it would move the flow rather than correct it. Upstream: EF 3.1 should point the flow at the Radioactivity property or reclassify it as a material resource.

`Water, salt, sole` is brine -- `Sole` is the German for a saturated salt solution, and the flow is a mixture of water and dissolved salts. 7732-18-5 is the registry number of the water molecule, and a mixture does not have the CAS of one of its constituents any more than seawater has oxygen's. Carrying it makes every downstream rule that keys on chemistry treat brine as water: the layering grouped it onto the water flow object until the material axis stopped that, and the semantic typing still concluded `chemrof:NeutralMolecule` from it, which contradicts the `ImpreciseChemicalMixture` the taxonomy states. 7727-37-9 is dinitrogen -- N2, the gas that is 78% of the air, indexed by Common Chemistry as `Nitrogen` with structure `N#N` and synonyms `Molecular nitrogen` and `Azote`. `Nitrogen, organic bound` is not a compound at all: it is the nitrogen held inside the organic matter of a discharge -- proteins, urea, amino acids -- reported as a mass of nitrogen, one of the standard nutrient-load quantities a wastewater plant measures. No registry number can name it, because a registry number names one compound and this is a measurement over many. So the number is not corrected here, it is removed: there is nothing to correct it to.

What the shared number did: this project treats a shared registry number as proof of shared identity, so EF's 5 `Nitrogen, organic bound` rows and its 13 `dinitrogen` rows were fused onto one flow object, the naming step renamed the organic-bound rows `Dinitrogen`, and ecoinvent's own `Nitrogen, organic bound` rows -- which carry the same wrong number, and from 3.9.1 carry `dinitrogen` among their synonyms as well -- then landed on them by CAS. A reader looking up organic-bound nitrogen was told it is nitrogen gas, with nitrogen gas's structure. Nothing separates the two today: dinitrogen is the definition of inert and carries no characterisation factor, organic-bound nitrogen carries none either, so the contested-registry-number gate has no factors to compare and leaves the group undecided (#34). Merged, the two are one substance for whichever eutrophication factor is attached next -- to a record that is mostly dinitrogen rows, including releases to air and soil where the factor is meaningless.

With the number gone the rows group by name, which is what the pesticide groupings do, and the semantic typing types the object `brightway:AggregateMeasurement` -- the same answer it gives `Phosphorus, Total` and `Chemical Oxygen Demand`. That answer came from a regex over the label when this fix was written and is a curated entry in `aggregate-measurements.json` since #68, which is why the removal here is still necessary and no longer sufficient on its own. The four water-context collisions this fusion produced in the `elementary-flow-collision` queue go with it. Matched on name because EF repeats the substance once per context, 5 rows in total. ecoinvent states the same removal in each of its five fixes files. Worth reporting upstream to EF. (#57, #44, #34)

EF 3.1 publishes one dye thirteen times, once per environmental compartment, and gives each copy a different name: `basic violet 1` through `basic violet 13`. All thirteen carry the same registry number, the same synonym list and the same structure, and their factors move the way one substance's factors move -- freshwater ecotoxicity 673.39, 674.86, 675.3 and 676.32 across the four air compartments, 974.07 in each of the three soils, 2268.5 in fresh and in unspecified water, zero in the two long-term ones. The digits are counting compartments, not naming substances.

`Basic Violet` is a Colour Index catalogue position and not a chemical family, so the other twelve names are twelve other dyes, and the registry says so itself. Asked for each of the thirteen names in turn, Common Chemistry answers with a different registry number every time: `basic violet 1` returns 8004-87-3 Methyl violet, `basic violet 2` returns 3248-91-7 New Fuchsin, `basic violet 3` returns 548-62-9 Crystal violet, `basic violet 4` returns 2390-59-2 Ethyl violet, `basic violet 10` returns 81-88-9 Rhodamine B, `basic violet 11` returns 2390-63-8 Rhodamine 3B. Exactly one of the thirteen names denotes the substance the rows carry.

Two of those other dyes are already in reach of this build, and the wrong names are pulling their identities toward these flows. EF 3.1 publishes crystal violet correctly as `C.I. Basic Violet 3` across its own thirteen compartments -- including `Emissions to air, indoor`, where its `c.i. basic violet 3` row (freshwater ecotoxicity 1754.1) sits in the same compartment as a `basic violet 3` row of methyl violet (675.3). `consensus_match` proposed ethyl violet's number for the `basic violet 4` row and only the conflict guard declined it (`blocked_name_update`); the `basic violet 7` row drew 6441-82-3, an unrelated cyanine dye, and was declined as `no_consensus_cas`. And `strip_cross_object_altlabels` was taking `Basic Violet 3` off crystal violet and `Basic Violet 10` off rhodamine B, because those names were the preferred labels of flows that are neither -- the guard against two substances sharing a name was firing, and firing on the correct substances.

8004-87-3 is methyl violet, and `C.I. Basic Violet 1` is what Common Chemistry names it -- so exactly one of the thirteen names was right, by the accident of being first. GLAD's ILCD/EF 3.1 to SimaPro 10.2 correspondence, mapped and verified by PRe Sustainability, reads the rows the same way: all thirteen uuids map to a single SimaPro flow, `C.I. Basic violet 1`, while EF's crystal violet rows map to `C.I. Basic violet 3`. The `C.I.` spelling is EF's own for the other dye, so the two now read alike.

Stated once against the registry number because it is one statement about one substance. No characterisation factor moves -- each stays on the flow and the compartment EF published it for -- and the grouping does not change either: the thirteen were already one flow object, whose preferred label was `Basic Violet 10`, which in the Colour Index is Rhodamine B. So the substance was published under the name of a dye it is not, showing methyl violet's structure and methyl violet's number. The names are wrong in EF 3.1's own published list and the collision with its own `C.I. Basic Violet 3` is there before it is here; worth reporting upstream, as plans/contested-cas.md already suggests for this number. (#280)

EF 3.1 ships CAS 65381-09-1 under two names: twelve flows are `Glycerol octanoate decanoate` and this one, the emission to agricultural soil, is `Decanoic acid, ester with 1,2,3-propanetriol octanoate`. Common Chemistry holds both for that number -- the record is `Glyceryl caprylate caprate` and lists the systematic form as a synonym -- so the two name one substance and nothing has to be decided about identity here. What has to be decided is which of them the object publishes, because the flow object takes its label from whichever member name sorts first, and that was this one: thirteen flows named in three words each were being presented under a fourteen-word name that one of them carried. Matched on UUID because it is the only flow that needs moving; the other twelve are already right. The systematic name is not lost -- the Common Chemistry synonym pass adds it as an altLabel on the object regardless of this fix, and the paired `reject` ruling in preferred-label-decisions.json stops the rename rule pushing the other twelve the other way.

EF 3.1 publishes fluorescein's disodium salt thirteen times, once per environmental compartment, and names twelve of the copies after a different substance. Twelve rows are `Fluorescein` or `fluorescein`, which is the free acid -- CAS 2321-07-5, C20H12O5, InChIKey GNBHRKFJIUUOQI-UHFFFAOYSA-N, 332 g/mol. The thirteenth, the emission to agricultural soil, is `disodium 2-(3-oxo-6-oxidoxanthen-9-yl)benzoate`, which is the salt spelled out the long way.

Three of EF's own fields say the salt and only the name says otherwise. All thirteen rows carry CAS 518-47-8 and EC 208-253-0, and both of those numbers are the salt's. All thirteen carry the same general comment: `Flow name and second synonym interchanged with each other`, which is EF saying that the string in the name field is a synonym that was swapped in. And the acid is not merely absent from the identifiers -- it is present in the synonym list, as `Fluorescein (free acid)`, `Fluorescein acid` and the truncated InChIKey `GNBHRKFJIUUOQI-UHFFFAOYSA-`, beside `Fluorescein sodium`, `Fluorescein disodium salt` and `Uranin` for the salt. So the row describes both substances and its identifiers pick one. This build's own enrichment agrees with the identifiers rather than with the name: the object publishes C20H12Na2O5, MOUPEUAUBSXMLI-UHFFFAOYSA-N and 378.29 g/mol, with the two sodium atoms in it, and OPSIN reads the IUPAC name as `... 3',6'-dihydroxy-, disodium salt`.

`Fluorescein sodium` is what Common Chemistry holds for 518-47-8, alongside `Sodium fluorescein` and `Fluorescein, disodium salt`, and it is what the pharmacopoeias call the substance. It is chosen over the systematic name because both are the salt's and one of them is readable in three words; the systematic form stays reachable, since the Common Chemistry synonym pass adds it as an altLabel whatever the preferred label is. The paired `reject` ruling in `preferred-label-decisions.json` stops the rename rule pushing the thirteen back the other way, the same arrangement `Glycerol octanoate decanoate` uses.

The replaced name is deliberately *not* retained as an alternative label. `retain_original_as_synonym` asserts that the string being replaced is a name the substance genuinely has, and bare `Fluorescein` is not one: every fluorescein name Common Chemistry holds for 518-47-8 qualifies it -- `Fluorescein sodium`, `Disodium fluorescein`, `Soluble Fluorescein`, `Fluorescein, soluble` -- and the unqualified word belongs to 2321-07-5. Keeping it would publish, as a thing this substance is called, the exact confusion the fix is correcting, and would let a later row named `Fluorescein` match the salt on a name. Nothing is stranded by leaving it off: no list other than EF 3.1 reaches these thirteen flows.

Stated once against the registry number because it is one statement about one substance. No characterisation factor moves and no grouping changes: the thirteen were already one flow object, whose preferred label was the systematic name because that name sorts before `Fluorescein`. The name is wrong in EF 3.1's own published list, and EF's own comment says a swap happened, so it is worth reporting upstream. (#312)

12447-40-4 is borax -- Common Chemistry names it `Borax (B4Na2O7.10H2O)` and all 24 of its synonyms are borax's, from `Borax decahydrate` to `20 Mule Team Borax`. EF 3.1 puts that number on seven rows: one it names `borax`, in Resource -> Ground, and six it names `Borate` -- five water compartments and Resource -> Ground again. Borate is the ion; borax is one particular salt of it. Borax is sodium tetraborate decahydrate, Na2B4O7 with ten waters, mined as a mineral and used as a flux, a detergent builder and a wood preservative. A borate resource flow is boron reported as the ion, whatever mineral it came out of. The two are not interchangeable in an inventory: a kilogram of borax is about a fifth boron by mass. Sharing the number is what puts all seven on one flow object, which is then typed `chemrof:ChemicalSalt` and published under the ion's name, so the list currently says that a borate resource is borax and gives it borax's structure and trade names. It also doubles Resource -> Ground, which is what put this pair in the `elementary-flow-collision` queue. ecoinvent tells the two apart and this project should too: ecoinvent reaches the borax row as `Borax` under 12447-40-4's cousin 1303-96-4 (3.12) and 1330-43-4 (3.8), and its own `Borate` rows carry 11129-12-7, the borate ion. No mapping is lost by the separation, because both sides arrive through the correspondence table on uuid rather than on the number. Nothing is asserted about what the borate rows *are*: the number is removed rather than replaced, which is the repair #57 made when EF and ecoinvent gave organic-bound nitrogen the registry number of nitrogen gas. (#106) Matched on the name alone: a fix that also matched on the number it removes cannot match a second time, and the base list applies its fixes twice (#237), so the second pass would report it as having gone stale.

Note that the CAS No is the relevant identifier, to which also the ILCD LCIA characterisation factors relate." That is the source telling a reader to trust the number over the name, which is what this correction does: the number is kept and the name is corrected to the substance the number names.

The substance the plain name belongs to is in EF 3.1 already, in all thirteen compartments, under its systematic name `1,1'-dimethyl-4,4'-bipyridinium`, 4685-14-7, EC 225-141-7 -- and that flow's synonyms include `PARAQUAT`, `Paraquat [ANSI:BSI:ISO]`, `Paraquat ion` and `Paraquat dication`. So nothing is lost by taking the bare name off the salt: the right flow exists everywhere the wrong one does.

Matched on the registry number rather than on the name, because the number is the half of the row this project has decided is right, and because EF spells the name in one case here but recapitalises the same substance elsewhere -- keying on a spelling would be keying on the thing that is wrong. Thirteen flows, one per compartment.

`retain_original_as_synonym` is deliberately not set. The flag asserts that the replaced string is a name the substance genuinely has; `Paraquat` is a name of a different chemical, which is the whole of the defect, and publishing it as an alternative label would leave every list that maps onto EF 3.1 by name landing here exactly as before. EF's own spelling is not lost either way: every flow records it as `elementary_flow_sources.source_flow_name`, so an inventory written against EF's uuid still resolves. (#119)

EF 3.1 calls thirteen flows `1,3,5-triazine`, one per compartment, and writes 121-82-4 on every one of them. That number is RDX's, the explosive hexahydro-1,3,5-trinitro-1,3,5-triazine; the bare ring the name describes is 290-87-9. EF's own row says which substance it means. Its EC number, 204-500-1, is RDX's. Its thirty-odd synonyms are all RDX's -- `rdx`, `cyclonite`, `hexogen`, `hexahydro-1,3,5-trinitro-1,3,5-triazine`, `1,3,5-trinitro-1,3,5-triazinane` -- and the plain name appears in none of them except as the stem of a longer RDX name. USEtox 2.1, where EF's three toxicity categories come from, carries 121-82-4 as `1,3,5,-trinitrohexahydro-1,3,5-triazine`, so the factors EF publishes on these flows are RDX's too. The name is the one field on the row that disagrees with the rest of it, which is the paraquat shape above: the number is kept and the name corrected to the substance the number names, under Common Chemistry's index name for it.

Matched on the registry number rather than the name for the same reasons as paraquat, and because the number is on thirteen flows and the name on exactly those thirteen. `retain_original_as_synonym` is deliberately not set: `1,3,5-triazine` is the name of a different chemical, and keeping it as an alternative label would leave any list shipping the real triazine landing here by name. Stepwise 2006 is that list -- six rows named `1,3,5-Triazine` under 290-87-9, which reached this object through its preferred label because nothing held their number. With the name corrected they find nothing and mint the substance they are. EF's own spelling survives on every flow as `elementary_flow_sources.source_flow_name`. (#199)

MCPA is a herbicide. The chemical called MCPA is an acid, 94-74-6; 3653-48-3 is its sodium salt, which is a different chemical sold at a different rate. EF 3.1 ships both and puts the plain name on the salt, over thirteen flows.

Every other field on those flows says sodium salt. The registry number is 3653-48-3 and the EC number is 222-895-9, both the salt's, and the synonym list EF ships is nothing but salt names: `MCPA-sodium`, `MCPA sodium salt`, `Sodium MCPA`, `Acetic acid, 2-(4-chloro-2-methylphenoxy)-, sodium salt (1:1)`, and the products `Chwastox`, `Dikotex` and `Methoxone sodium salt`. These flows carry the same general comment as EF's paraquat rows -- "Note that the CAS No is the relevant identifier, to which also the ILCD LCIA characterisation factors relate" -- so the source itself says the number decides and the name is what slipped.

The acid is in EF 3.1 already, in all thirteen compartments, as `2-methyl-4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid`, 94-74-6, EC 202-360-6, carrying `MCPA` and `MCPA [BSI:ISO]` among its synonyms. So correcting the salt's name costs nothing: whatever means MCPA has a flow to reach in every compartment.

`MCPA-sodium` rather than a systematic spelling, because it is the name ecoinvent already uses for this substance -- its `MCPA-sodium` flow carries 3653-48-3 in seven compartments -- and it is in EF's own synonym list for the number. Two lists agreeing on a name is the argument AGENTS.md 35 asks for.

Matched on the registry number, because EF spells this one `MCPA` on eleven flows and `mcpa` on two, and a fix keyed on a spelling would catch one group and miss the other. Thirteen flows in total.

`retain_original_as_synonym` is deliberately not set: `MCPA` names the acid, and asserting it as an alternative name for the salt is the confusion this corrects. Two of the thirteen flows already ship the lower-case string `mcpa` in their own synonym list, so the abbreviation still names two substances in the extracted data; #113's rule -- a synonym that names two substances is published for neither -- is what withdraws it, and this correction is about the preferred name rather than about that list. (#119)

Flupyrsulfuron-methyl is a herbicide, 144740-53-4; 144740-54-5 is its sodium salt. EF 3.1 ships only the salt -- 144740-54-5 on thirteen flows, one per compartment, and no flow anywhere in the list carrying 144740-53-4 -- and it names those thirteen after the parent, `Flupyrsulfuron-methyl` on one and `flupyrsulfuron-methyl` on the other twelve.

There is nothing to weigh against the number here. These flows carry no EC number, no synonyms and no general comment: the registry number is the only identifying material EF ships, and it is the salt's. ecoinvent names the same number `Flupyrsulfuron-methyl sodium`, in seven compartments of 3.11 and 3.12, and ships the parent acid separately under 144740-53-4 -- so one list distinguishes the two substances by name and the other does not.

This correction is the one that makes the routing correction possible. ecoinvent's parent-acid rows have no right flow in EF 3.1 to reach, so `ecoinvent-match-overrides.json` declines their published mapping and lets them mint a consensus flow of their own. A declined row falls through to matching on the evidence it carries, and while EF's salt flow is called `flupyrsulfuron-methyl` the evidence includes an exact name match with a substance the row is not. Correcting the name is what leaves the registry numbers to decide, which is the right answer for both rows: 144740-54-5 finds the salt and 144740-53-4 finds nothing.

Matched on the registry number rather than the name, for the same reason as the four corrections above -- the name is the field that is wrong, and it is spelled two ways. Thirteen flows.

`retain_original_as_synonym` is deliberately not set: `Flupyrsulfuron-methyl` names the parent acid, which is a substance ecoinvent ships and this list publishes, and retaining it here would restate the confusion the rename removes. (#119)

Gypsum is calcium sulfate that has taken up water: two water molecules per formula unit, 13397-24-5. Drive the water off and what is left is anhydrite, the same salt without it, 7778-18-9. They are two minerals, mined and traded separately, and a tonne of one is not a tonne of the other. This flow is EF 3.1's only resource-from-ground flow for either, it carries 7778-18-9, and it is named `gypsum`.

Every synonym EF ships on this flow is a name of the dry salt: `Anhydrite`, `Anhydrous calcium sulfate`, `Anhydrous gypsum`, `Anhydrous sulfate of lime`, `Natural anhydrite`, `Karstenite`, `Muriacite`, `Calcium sulfate, anhydrous` and `CaSO4`. Nothing in the row describes the hydrate except the name.

EF 3.1 also ships the same substance a second time, correctly named. Its thirteen emission flows called `calcium sulfate` carry the same 7778-18-9, with EC 231-900-3. So the list already holds the right name for this number, and this correction is EF being made to agree with itself rather than a name brought in from outside.

`Calcium sulfate` rather than `Anhydrite`, for that reason: it is EF's own name for the number everywhere else in the list, and it is what this project already publishes for the substance -- ecoinvent's own resource flow for 7778-18-9 is called `Anhydrite`, and this list already renames it to `Calcium sulfate`. `Anhydrite` stays reachable either way: it is the fifth synonym on this row and it is ecoinvent's own spelling.

Matched on the uuid rather than on the registry number, which is the exception to the rule the four corrections above follow. 7778-18-9 is on fourteen EF flows: this one and the thirteen already named `calcium sulfate`. Keying on the number would restate the correct name on thirteen rows that do not need it, and a fix that mostly changes nothing is a fix whose effect nobody can read in a diff.

`retain_original_as_synonym` is deliberately not set, and here it is the whole point. `Gypsum` names the hydrate, which is a different mineral with its own registry number; retaining it would leave every list that maps onto EF 3.1 by name sending its gypsum rows to anhydrite, which is what ecoinvent's and BAFU's gypsum rows do today. (#119)

Mecoprop comes as a fifty-fifty mixture of two mirror-image forms of the same molecule. Only one of the two kills weeds, and the pure active form is sold as mecoprop-P, at half the dose of the mixture. They are two products with two registry numbers, and EF 3.1 puts the name of the pure form on the mixture, over thirteen flows.

Every synonym EF ships with them is the mixture's: `mecoprop`, `mecoprop(iso)`, `mcpp`, `(rs)-2-(4-chloro-o-tolyloxy)propionic acid` and `(+-)-2-((4-Chloro-o-tolyl)oxy)propionic acid`. The prefixes `(rs)-` and `(+-)-` are how a chemist writes "both mirror images, in equal amounts", which is the one thing mecoprop-P is not.

The pure form is in EF 3.1 already, in eleven compartments as `(R)-2-(4-chloro-2-methylphenoxy)propionic acid` and in the remaining two under the same name in lower case, all thirteen carrying 16484-77-8 and EC 240-539-0 -- with `Mecoprop-P`, `(R)-Mecoprop` and `d-Mecoprop` among their synonyms. Common Chemistry names 16484-77-8 `(+)-Mecoprop` and gives it InChIKey WNTGYJSOUMFZEP-SSDOTTSWSA-N, against WNTGYJSOUMFZEP-UHFFFAOYSA-N for the unresolved parent: the same skeleton, one with the mirror image fixed and one without. So the substance the name belongs to is available in every compartment the mislabelled flow is.

`Mecoprop` rather than the systematic name, because it is the ISO common name, it is Common Chemistry's own name for the substance, it is what ecoinvent and BAFU both call their own flows for it, and it is already the second synonym EF ships on these very rows.

Matched on the name rather than on the registry number, which is the opposite of the four corrections above and is deliberate. The number on these rows is corrected too, by the two entries below, so a criterion that read it would match nothing on the second pass the base list makes over its own fixes (#237) and would report itself stale. A rename keyed on the name it replaces is the one shape `apply_manual_fixes` recognises as already applied instead. All thirteen flows spell it `mecoprop-p`, so one criterion reaches every one of them, and no other EF 3.1 flow is named `mecoprop` or `mecoprop-p`.

`retain_original_as_synonym` is deliberately not set: `mecoprop-p` names the pure enantiomer, which is a different substance with its own thirteen flows in this same list, and keeping the string as a synonym here would leave a name-matching step free to send mecoprop-P's rows to the mixture, which is the routing defect this correction exists to stop. (#119)

EF 3.1 files mecoprop under 7085-19-0, and the number in current use is 93-65-2. This is the borax shape from #110 exactly: nobody disagrees about what the substance is, the two halves of the list simply never meet, because the reference databases file it under the current number while the flow holds the older one.

Common Chemistry says so in the plainest way available. Asked for 7085-19-0 it returns a record whose own registry number is **93-65-2**, named `Mecoprop`, formula C10H11ClO3, InChIKey WNTGYJSOUMFZEP-UHFFFAOYSA-N -- that is the service resolving the older entry onto the current one rather than holding two substances. ChEBI files the same molecule under 93-65-2 as well, as `2-(4-chloro-2-methylphenoxy)propanoic acid`, CHEBI:75704.

Every other list this project merges already uses the current number. ecoinvent carries 93-65-2 on its `Mecoprop` flow in 3.8 and in 3.11 and 3.12 -- eight rows between them -- and BAFU 2026-v1 carries it on its own `Mecoprop` row. EF 3.1 is the only one of the three holding 7085-19-0, and no EF 3.1 flow carries 93-65-2, checked over all 94,062 flows of the extracted input of 20 August 2026, so nothing collides with the corrected number.

What it buys is the difference between a name and a number. Before this, the renamed flow and ecoinvent's rows agreed only on the string `Mecoprop`, so the merge placed eight ecoinvent rows and one BAFU row on it with `basis=label` -- a match on the evidence of last resort, across a registry-number disagreement. With the number corrected they agree on the number, and the same rows arrive on `basis=cas`. It also answers the question the rename raised: the build's `cas-ambiguous` queue reported this flow's name matching a ChEBI record whose number the flow did not carry, which is the shape that queue takes whenever the disagreement is about vintage rather than identity.

Matched on the corrected name rather than on the number, for the reason the borax correction gives: the number is the field being changed, and a criterion that reads it matches nothing on the second pass the base list makes over its own fixes (#237). `original_value` is what makes that pass a quiet no-op rather than a stale-fix warning. Ordered after the rename above, so the criterion sees the corrected name. (#119)

The other half of the renumbering, and it has to move with it. ECHA's EC inventory carries the same molecule twice under two entries, and it pairs each with one registry number: 230-386-8 is `Mecoprop`, 7085-19-0, and 202-264-4 is `2-(4-chloro-2-methylphenoxy)propionic acid`, 93-65-2 -- both C10H11ClO3, read from the inventory this project ships (`ec-inventory.json.gz`, 106,213 records, downloaded 2026-02-22). Moving the registry number to 93-65-2 and leaving EC 230-386-8 behind would make the row state a pair ECHA does not pair, and the EC index decides identity downstream exactly as the registry number does.

That the two entries are one substance is not an inference from the formula: PubChem's record for it links both ECHA infocards, 100.002.060 and 100.027.624, which are 202-264-4 and 230-386-8, and the published flow object already carries both URLs as references.

No EF 3.1 flow carries 202-264-4, so nothing collides. Matched on the corrected name and guarded by `original_value`, for the same reasons as the entry above. (#119)

fixes.new_value: Mecoprop, the herbicide, registry number 93-65-2. It is a fifty-fifty mixture of two mirror-image forms of one molecule, only one of which kills weeds; the pure active form is sold as mecoprop-P, is applied at half the dose, and is a different substance with its own thirteen flows in this list under 16484-77-8. EF 3.1 ships these rows named `mecoprop-p`, which is the pure form's name, and registered 7085-19-0 with EC 230-386-8, which is a superseded filing for the mixture. The name and both numbers are corrected here: an inventory written against EF 3.1 that carries 7085-19-0 or 230-386-8 means this flow.
fixes.comment: Says on the published row what the renumbering leaves unsaid, which is the arrangement #106 and #110 used for borax. This project has no structured place to record a superseded registry number -- `cas_numbers` holds what the substance *is*, and a second number in it would be read as a second identity by every rule that keys on chemistry -- so the number EF shipped survives in prose or not at all. A reader who comes to this flow holding 7085-19-0, which is what EF 3.1 published and what an inventory written against EF 3.1 may carry, has otherwise no way to tell that this is the same flow. Thirteen rows, which had no general comment of their own. (#119)

Arsenate is what arsenic(5+) is called when it is dissolved in water, which is where an inventory almost always reports it: As(V) does not exist as a bare cation in solution but as the oxyanion AsO4(3-). Somebody looking up an arsenate release should find this substance, and today the word appears nowhere on it -- EF ships these thirteen flows as `arsenic (v)` with the one synonym `element in usetox`, which is a note about the model rather than a name.

**Added as a synonym and not as the name.** The flow says a release of ionic arsenic in the +5 state; what that arsenic goes on to become in the receiving water is speciation chemistry the inventory does not state and this list should not assert. `Arsenic(5+)` names the thing released, `arsenate` is what a reader will search for, and the two are the same substance under EF's own identification -- 17428-41-0, on all thirteen flows.

Matched on the registry number rather than the name, as the other synonym fixes on this file are, so it reaches every one of the thirteen without naming them. (#127)

1345-04-6 is antimony trisulfide, Sb2S3 -- the compound stibnite ore is made of. EF 3.1 ships these thirteen flows under the systematic name `tricyclo[3.3.1.1~3,7~]tetrastibathiane`, which describes a four-antimony cage and is not Sb2S3, while giving them 1345-04-6 and the synonym `antimonysulphide`. So EF's own name and its own number disagree about which substance the flow is, and its synonym agrees with the number.

That is the shape #121 found in the trichloroethanes and #19 in the refrigerants, and it is settled the same way: this project trusts the registry number, and the name is corrected to the one the number denotes. `Antimony trisulfide` rather than `Stibnite`, because stibnite is the *mineral* -- the naturally occurring form -- and these thirteen flows are emissions, where the compound is what is meant. The mineral is what ecoinvent extracts from the ground, and it reaches this substance by registry number with a resource flow minted for it (#123).

Found by declining ecoinvent's `Stibnite` row: with the correspondence table no longer sending it to the antimonite ion, the row matched EF on 1345-04-6 and the published name became the cage compound's. The chemistry improved and the name got worse, which is what this corrects.

EF 3.1's own material peat, and the flow the renamed ecoinvent rows join. EF 3.1 ships two peat flows and they are two substances. `peat` is a `Non-renewable energy resource from ground`, measured in megajoules, and carries the `Resource use, fossils` factor of 1.0 -- that is peat burned as a fuel, counted by its energy content. This one is a `Renewable material resource from biosphere`, measured in kilograms, and carries no factor: it is peat dug and sold as a growing medium, counted by its mass. A mass of horticultural peat and a megajoule of fuel peat are not one substance measured two ways, and the list said they were only because both were called some form of `peat`.

What that cost: ecoinvent's kilogram row reached the megajoule flow, so the match recorded a unit crossing and the ecoinvent Centre's own factor for it -- `Resource use, fossils`, 9.76 per kilogram, which is peat's calorific value -- stopped being published, because 9.76 per kilogram is wrong by an order of magnitude on a flow measured in megajoules. Named for what it is used for rather than where it is found, because `Peat, in ground` says where and the question here is which of the two peats this is. The vendor's own spelling is retained as an alternative label: an inventory written against these lists holds no other string for it. (#89)

EF 3.1 publishes two substances under the one name `1-pentene`. Thirteen flows, one per compartment, carry CAS 109-67-1 and EC 203-694-5, and those are pent-1-ene, the single molecule. The thirteen renamed here carry CAS 25377-72-4 and EC 246-916-6, which name pentene as a mixture of isomers: Common Chemistry's record for that number is `Pentene`, with `Amylene`, `Pentylene`, `n-Pentene` and `n-Amylene` beside it, and it holds no InChI and no InChIKey at all, which is what a registry number covering more than one structure looks like. The record for 109-67-1 is `1-Pentene` and does hold one, YWAKXRMUMFPDSH-UHFFFAOYSA-N. Both spellings are EF's own: the ILCD flow datasets for both numbers carry `<baseName xml:lang="en">1-pentene</baseName>`, and nothing but the CAS, the EC and the first two synonyms differs between them.

EF's own characterisation factors agree that the second set is not 1-pentene. For freshwater ecotoxicity the 25377-72-4 rows carry 0.00066397 CTUe/kg to urban air, 0.00053053 to unspecified air, 2.9221 to unspecified soil and 475.74 to unspecified water, and `cis-2-pentene` (627-20-3) and `trans-2-pentene` (646-04-8) carry those four numbers exactly -- a generic pentene factor applied to whichever isomer, rather than one molecule's own. 1-pentene's own four are 0.00031356, 0.00025056, 1.38 and 224.58, a factor of 2.1 below. Read off the 2026-08-25 build.

The build already reports the name as wrong, twice. All thirteen rows sit in the `commonchem-name-cas` queue, because the name `1-pentene` resolves in Common Chemistry to 109-67-1 while the row carries 25377-72-4, and the flow object sits in the `consensus-match` queue as `blocked_name_update`: the rename rule proposed `Pentene` and its own containment heuristic refused, reading `pentene` inside `1-pentene` as a broader-or-narrower pair.

`Pentylene` rather than Common Chemistry's own `Pentene`, because the point of the rename is that a reader can tell the two apart: `Pentene` is a substring of `1-pentene`, `2-pentene`, `Cis-2-pentene` and `Trans-2-pentene`, all of which this list publishes, and it is the very string the rename rule's containment check stumbled on. `Pentylene` is Common Chemistry's synonym for this number and no other substance's published name. The paired `reject` ruling in `preferred-label-decisions.json` stops the rename rule pushing it back to `Pentene`, the same arrangement `Fluorescein sodium` uses.

The replaced name is deliberately not retained as an alternative label. `retain_original_as_synonym` asserts that the replaced string is a name the substance genuinely has, and `1-pentene` is 109-67-1's name -- this list publishes that substance under it, so keeping it here would republish the ambiguity the fix removes, and the carry-member-names pass drops a string that answers for two substances anyway (#113). Nothing is stranded by leaving it off: `Pentene`, `n-Pentene` and `Pentylene` already reach the object as alternative labels from the Common Chemistry synonym pass, and no list but EF 3.1 reaches these thirteen flows -- ecoinvent 3.8, ecoinvent 3.12 and BAFU 2026-v1 all send their `1-Pentene` rows to 109-67-1.

Stated once against the registry number because it is one statement about one substance. No factor moves and no grouping changes: the thirteen were already one flow object. The duplicate name is in EF 3.1's published list, so it is worth reporting upstream. (#157)

`Silicium` is the Latin name for the element, and EF 3.1 is the only list here that uses it for SiF4. CAS Common Chemistry publishes 7783-61-1 as `Silicon tetrafluoride`; PubChem's CID 24556 gives `tetrafluorosilane` as the IUPAC preferred name and carries `Silicon tetrafluoride` among its synonyms; ChEBI has no record of the compound at all, and the only `silicium` in its 224,571 nodes is a foreign-language synonym of the element itself (CHEBI:27573, beside `Silizium` and `silicio`). ecoinvent, BAFU and AGRIBALYSE 3.2 all write `Silicon tetrafluoride`. That is three contributing lists and the registry against one spelling, which is what §6 of the conventions settles by taking the name the other lists use.

The rename rule cannot reach this one: `cc_chebi_agreement` requires Common Chemistry and ChEBI to agree, and ChEBI has nothing to agree with, so the label stayed as `bootstrap_labels` wrote it from EF's own name field and never came up for a ruling. The build has been reporting the difference on the `commonchem-cas-name-differences` queue, one row per flow, for as long as the queue has existed (#187).

EF's spelling is retained as a synonym, so an inventory keyed on `Silicium Tetrafluoride` still finds the substance. `Tetrafluorosilane` and `Silicon tetrafluoride` are already alternative labels on the object, written by `consensus_match` from the CAS lookup, so no synonym needs adding.
